title: Largest rectangle in a histogram
prompt: Write largestRectangleArea(heights []int) int: the area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle that fits entirely under a histogram whose bars each have width 1. An empty histogram has area 0. It must run in O(n): the tests feed a strictly increasing staircase of 500000 bars, where expanding outwards from every bar costs O(n^2) and never finishes.
explanation: The stack holds indices whose heights are increasing, so for the bar on top the previous stack entry is already its first strictly smaller bar on the left, and the bar you are about to push is its first smaller bar on the right. Both boundaries arrive for free, which is why each bar is pushed once and popped once and the whole scan is O(n). Two details carry the correctness. The width is i - left - 1, not i - top, because the rectangle at height heights[top] spreads all the way back to just after the entry below it on the stack, covering every bar popped before it. And the loop runs to i == len(heights) with a sentinel height of 0 so that bars still on the stack at the end, which have no smaller bar to their right, get flushed against the right edge. Using >= rather than > when popping equal heights is safe: the shorter-lived duplicate reports a narrow area, and the last of the equal run reaches back past all of them.
hints: For each bar, what two indices do you need before you can compute its rectangle?
What ordering would you have to keep on the stack so the entry underneath is already one of those boundaries?
What happens to the bars still on the stack when the scan ends, and how can you avoid writing that as a second loop?

title: Edit distance
prompt: Write minDistance(a, b string) int returning the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn a into b. Either string may be empty. The tests run 4000-byte strings, so the plain recursion is out; they also plant a known number of substitutions, so a solution that only inserts and deletes reports twice the right answer.
explanation: dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i bytes of a and the first j bytes of b. If the two current bytes match, nothing needs paying and dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise you pay one for whichever of the three moves is cheapest: dp[i-1][j-1] is a substitution, dp[i-1][j] is deleting a[i-1], dp[i][j-1] is inserting b[j-1]. The base row and column are j and i, since turning a string into the empty string costs one deletion per byte. Each cell reads only the row above and the cell to its left, so two rows are enough and the space drops from O(n*m) to O(m); that is the only reason the 4000x4000 case is comfortable. Dropping the diagonal-plus-one term gives the longest-common-subsequence distance instead, which counts a substitution as a delete and an insert, and is exactly the wrong answer the planted test catches.
hints: Define the subproblem over prefixes of both strings before writing any loop.
When the two current bytes differ, three moves are available. Which table entry does each one leave you looking at?
Which rows of the table does a cell actually read? That answers how much of it you need to keep.
refs: LC 583 Delete Operation for Two Strings

title: Maximum flow
prompt: Write maxFlow(n, edges [][]int, s, t int) int. edges holds {from, to, capacity} triples for directed arcs over nodes 0..n-1; parallel arcs are allowed and capacities go up to a billion. Return the maximum flow from s to t. The tests cross-check small networks against a brute-forced minimum cut, so a greedy that saturates paths without ever being able to undo them will not pass, and they include a 2000-by-2000 bipartite matching.
explanation: Every arc is stored with a paired reverse arc of capacity 0, and pushing f along an arc subtracts f from it and adds f to its partner. That reverse arc is the whole trick: sending flow back along it cancels an earlier decision, which is what lets a greedy first choice be repaired later, and it is why the min-cut cross-check fails any solution that omits it. Dinic then adds two ideas on top of plain augmentation. A BFS from s labels every node with its distance in the residual graph, and the DFS is only allowed to step from level d to level d+1, so every augmenting path found in a phase is a shortest one. Within a phase, iter[u] remembers how far through u's arc list the DFS has already looked and is never rewound, and a node that yields nothing has its level cleared, so each arc is examined once per phase; that makes a phase O(V*E) and the shortest-path length strictly increases between phases, giving O(V^2 * E) overall and O(E * sqrt(V)) when all capacities are 1. Pushing the bottleneck of the path rather than one unit is what keeps the billion-capacity case to a handful of rounds.
hints: What has to be true of the graph you search so that an early, wrong-looking assignment of flow can still be corrected later?
If you always take a shortest augmenting path, what happens to that length across rounds, and why does that bound the work?
Within one round, what can you remember about each node so its arcs are never rescanned?
